article_ideas.audience: Infrastructure strategists, capacity planners, and data-center operators
article_ideas.based_on: Energy production constraints are the ultimate physical limitation on scaling AI data centers.
article_ideas.thesis: When a layer of the AI stack saturates, the binding constraint moves down the stack to the hardest-to-substitute layer — from accelerators to power and grid access — so scaling roadmaps should be planned against the lowest layer, not the most talked-about one.
article_ideas.title: Where the Constraint Migrates
article_ideas.video_title: Jensen Huang Thinks A.I. Alarmism Has Gone Too Far | The Ezra Klein Show

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the famous counter-example as a boundary-condition result and ask which professions share its elasticity profile.
article_ideas.audience: Workforce strategists, product leaders modeling automation ROI, and policy analysts
article_ideas.based_on: Radiologists using AI tools to process more scans and handle more cases, increasing demand for radiologists.
article_ideas.thesis: The radiology case is not evidence that task automation preserves employment in general; it is evidence that it preserves employment where the human bottleneck is throughput-bound and residual demand is elastic — which makes the counter-example conditional, not universal.
article_ideas.title: Automation Only Expands a Job Where Demand Is Elastic
article_ideas.video_title: Jensen Huang Thinks A.I. Alarmism Has Gone Too Far | The Ezra Klein Show

article_ideas.angle: Quantitative reliability engineering for AI pipelines: model error amplification, derive per-stage accuracy budgets, and argue against treating ingestion as a pre-processing afterthought.
article_ideas.audience: AI reliability engineers, ML platform teams building agentic workflows
article_ideas.based_on: errors compound across sequential decisions
article_ideas.thesis: In multi-step agent pipelines, upstream data errors multiply across sequential decisions rather than averaging out, so ingestion fidelity requirements scale with pipeline depth—making the earliest shared input the highest-leverage reliability investment.
article_ideas.title: The Error-Compounding Tax: Why Agentic Pipelines Force a New Ingestion Accuracy Bar
article_ideas.video_title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto

article_ideas.angle: Architecture argument: the 'parse' stage becomes a routing artifact, forcing index/context stores to diverge and formatting to get its own evaluation.
article_ideas.audience: RAG architects, AI engineers building retrieval systems
article_ideas.based_on: Serve documents in multiple representations split by consumer model
article_ideas.thesis: A single text extraction cannot serve both embedding models and LLMs; production pipelines must emit multiple, explicitly routed views (HTML for reasoning, natural language for retrieval) and accept the consistency/storage overhead as a first-class design cost.
article_ideas.title: Kill the Canonical Chunk: Consumer-Aware Document Representations for RAG and Agents
article_ideas.video_title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto

article_ideas.angle: Evidence-based caution against agent-in-the-loop hype; proposes a benchmark framework and threshold-setting methodology.
article_ideas.audience: Document AI product leaders, AI QA engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Agentic OCR replaces human-in-the-loop review with agent-in-the-loop
article_ideas.thesis: Autonomous token-level corrections introduce silent errors that are harder to detect than obvious OCR noise; replacing human review depends on measurable per-error-type precision/recall and explicit escalation policies, not capability demos.
article_ideas.title: Agentic OCR Won't Replace Human Review Until We Measure Correction Precision
article_ideas.video_title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto

article_ideas.angle: Practical architecture blueprint with cost/accuracy trade-offs, routing error analysis, and failure modes.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform architects, document ingestion engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Hybrid document understanding: cheap sub-100M-parameter CV models on CPU handle deterministic structure
article_ideas.thesis: Deterministic structure extraction belongs on CPU with small models while VLMs should handle only semantic long-tail cases; this boundary is a cost/latency design decision, and misrouting is a first-class error source that must be instrumented.
article_ideas.title: The Hybrid Ingestion Stack: Cost-Tiered CV + VLM as the Default Architecture
article_ideas.video_title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto

article_ideas.angle: Architecture argument backed by an ablation design comparing top-k vector-only retrieval against a full tool harness on multi-turn document QA.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers building RAG and agent systems
article_ideas.based_on: Retrieval is migrating out of the data layer and into the agent layer
article_ideas.thesis: The retrieval layer should expose composable tools and filesystem-like navigation to agents, because baking retrieval complexity into the agent layer improves multi-turn document QA more than tuning a single vector retriever; teams that keep a fixed top-k API will hit a ceiling on diverse enterprise corpora.
article_ideas.title: Retrieval Is Moving Into the Agent: Stop Treating RAG as a Top-K Endpoint
article_ideas.video_title: Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex

article_ideas.angle: Tradeoff analysis and benchmark-driven parser selection, treating routing logic as the core artifact.
article_ideas.audience: Document AI and infrastructure engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Document parsing has a Pareto frontier that no single approach reaches
article_ideas.thesis: No single document parser wins across enterprise document types, so the right engineering choice is a routed hybrid with deterministic pipeline parsers by default and selective VLM escalation for complex tables and charts, defended by a benchmark rather than vendor preference.
article_ideas.title: The Parser Pareto Frontier: Why Hybrid Routing Beats Choosing One Model
article_ideas.video_title: Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex

article_ideas.angle: Reliability and auditability argument for regulated-industry extraction systems.
article_ideas.audience: Enterprise AI, fintech, and insurtech engineers
article_ideas.based_on: output must be schema-based structured data with granular attribution back to source coordinates
article_ideas.thesis: High-stakes extraction is not a text-generation problem but an auditability problem; values must ship with source coordinates and calibrated confidence, otherwise an incorrect extraction is undetectable and catastrophic in finance and insurance.
article_ideas.title: Provenance Is the Product: Regulated Extraction Needs Bounding Boxes and Calibrated Confidence
article_ideas.video_title: Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex

article_ideas.angle: Engineering-process argument about the artifact shift from code-defined pipelines to natural-language orchestration.
article_ideas.audience: Agent platform engineers and engineering managers
article_ideas.based_on: Agent orchestration is moving from code-defined pipelines toward English-based runbooks
article_ideas.thesis: As agent orchestration moves from Python and TypeScript definitions to English runbooks, MCP configuration, and goal/rubric alignment, teams must treat runbooks and rubrics as version-controlled, testable engineering artifacts; otherwise agent behavior loses its review process and regression surface.
article_ideas.title: Runbooks Are Code: Versioning English Orchestration in Agent Systems
article_ideas.video_title: Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the agent-adoption conversation from capability benchmarking to environment curation, and give a concrete ordering: repo hygiene and interface standardization before broader write access, with guardrails treated as infrastructure rather than as a safety tax.
article_ideas.audience: Platform engineering leads, staff+ engineers running agent rollouts, and engineering managers deciding where to spend AI budget
article_ideas.based_on: Agent productivity is claimed to be bounded by the structure of the environment
article_ideas.thesis: Agent productivity is gated by the machine-readability and constraint density of the environment, not by model capability — so the engineering budget allocated to model and prompt tuning is being spent on the wrong variable while repo entropy, inconsistent interfaces, and missing guardrails set a hard ceiling that no model upgrade lifts.
article_ideas.title: Your Agents Are Not the Bottleneck. Your Repository Is.
article_ideas.video_title: Thinking in Platforms • Kasper von Grünberg & Luca Galante • GOTO 2026

article_ideas.angle: Argue for deployment gating as an engineering control, describe what must exist at the gate (context provisioning, standardized interfaces, policy enforcement), and warn that the sequencing pressure to shortcut it grows precisely as perceived agent value rises.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, SRE/reliability owners, and platform teams being asked to support agent deployments
article_ideas.based_on: Without platform guardrails, deploying AI agents leads to organizational failure and chaos
article_ideas.thesis: The intern-without-onboarding analogy has a sharper consequence than 'low productivity': unguarded agents fail as coordination breakdown — uncontrolled changes, inconsistent artifacts, rollback volume — which means the correct pre-condition for granting agent write access is platform readiness, not model quality, and platform capability becomes a scheduled dependency of every agent roadmap.
article_ideas.title: Guardrails Before Write Access: Treating the Platform as Agent Onboarding
article_ideas.video_title: Thinking in Platforms • Kasper von Grünberg & Luca Galante • GOTO 2026

article_ideas.angle: Push back on the habit of treating socialization as overhead and political work as separate from architecture, and translate it into reviewable artifacts: product roadmap ownership, adoption metrics, and continued sponsorship as an explicit program dependency.
article_ideas.audience: Platform product managers, principal engineers, and executives sponsoring internal platform programs
article_ideas.based_on: Many platforms fail due to poor social integration and lack of executive support rather than technical flaws.
article_ideas.thesis: If platform failure is predominantly social rather than technical, then adoptability and executive air cover are engineering inputs with the same status as latency and uptime — design for buy-in, fund the product-management layer, and instrument voluntary usage, because a platform nobody chooses to use has already failed regardless of its architecture.
article_ideas.title: Technically Correct Platforms Still Die: Sponsorship as a Reliability Requirement
article_ideas.video_title: Thinking in Platforms • Kasper von Grünberg & Luca Galante • GOTO 2026

article_ideas.angle: Turn an abstract balance question into a classification exercise: sort work into mechanics and judgment, apply golden paths only to the first, and treat exit hatches as a first-class platform feature rather than a compliance loophole.
article_ideas.audience: Platform architects, developer-experience teams, and agent-guardrail designers
article_ideas.based_on: Platforms standardize means of work to reduce redundant repetitive tasks while keeping creativity
article_ideas.thesis: The industrialization parallel is useful only because it comes with a scoping rule: standardization must target the repetitive substrate and leave the differentiating layer unconstrained — which means most guardrail designs fail by standardizing the wrong layer, constraining discretionary work for humans and agents alike while leaving the actual toil untouched.
article_ideas.title: Standardize the Mechanics, Not the Judgment
article_ideas.video_title: Thinking in Platforms • Kasper von Grünberg & Luca Galante • GOTO 2026

article_ideas.angle: Trace a single tool-call round trip and separate the bytes that exist for the machine from the bytes that exist for a human reader; show what disappears when the machine-facing layer returns typed decisions instead of prose.
article_ideas.audience: Agent and backend engineers designing internal agent interfaces
article_ideas.based_on: Traditional tool calling uses text generation as a bridge between machine execution and human interfaces, which is inefficient.
article_ideas.thesis: Using text generation as the bridge between machine execution and human interfaces couples backend agent logic to a human-readable format it never needed, and the fix is to make every internal decision boundary carry typed data, reserving prose for the boundaries where a human actually reads the output.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent's Control Flow Should Not Speak English
article_ideas.video_title: How To Build A Harness With Jev | A LangChain x TypeSafe Conversation

article_ideas.angle: Argue that any irreversible tool warrants an interception point between model intent and side effect, then enumerate the new obligations the harness owner inherits once that gate exists.
article_ideas.audience: Platform engineers and agent-safety practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: Jev middleware can intercept tool calls and block destructive actions based on defined safety criteria.
article_ideas.thesis: Tool-call safety expressed as system-prompt instructions is a probabilistic suggestion, while a pre-execution interception layer is a deterministic choke point; moving authorization into the call path changes who is accountable for irreversible actions and makes false-block behavior an explicit engineering concern rather than an emergent one.
article_ideas.title: The Harness Owns the Gate, Not the Prompt
article_ideas.video_title: How To Build A Harness With Jev | A LangChain x TypeSafe Conversation

article_ideas.angle: Treat routing as a heterogeneous-fleet problem: every mixed cheap/expensive fleet needs an explicit, logged routing decision, and the router's misroute rate is the metric that determines whether the fleet is worth having.
article_ideas.audience: AI infrastructure and cost-optimization engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Model router middleware uses Jev to select between fast and deep models based on prompt complexity.
article_ideas.thesis: Model routing is itself a decision, so the component that arbitrates between cheap and expensive models should be the cheapest and most auditable part of the runtime; a router that costs as much as the thing it routes is a net negative and should be replaced by static configuration.
article_ideas.title: The Cheapest Model in the Stack Should Be the Router
article_ideas.video_title: How To Build A Harness With Jev | A LangChain x TypeSafe Conversation

article_ideas.angle: Take the headline multipliers seriously as a claim and list the measurement conditions that would need to hold for them to survive contact with a production workload.
article_ideas.audience: Technical decision-makers evaluating model vendors
article_ideas.based_on: Jev is 200-200x faster and 40-400x cheaper than traditional LLMs for structured choices.
article_ideas.thesis: Comparative performance claims about decision models are only actionable when stated with a task set, a baseline, and a volume assumption; until then they should be treated as a hypothesis to test rather than a budget line, because the cost profile at production volumes can invert the ranking.
article_ideas.title: What Would Falsify a 200x Speed and 40x Cost Claim?
article_ideas.video_title: How To Build A Harness With Jev | A LangChain x TypeSafe Conversation

article_ideas.angle: Argue that cost observability, per-workflow token attribution, and retry/step limits are production infrastructure, and that unit-price metrics are actively misleading when consumption grows faster than price declines.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and infrastructure engineers, engineering finance partners, and CIO/CTO offices managing AI budgets
article_ideas.based_on: Unit inference price is falling while total token consumption grows roughly 2,000% CAGR
article_ideas.thesis: The classic cloud cost playbook — wait for unit prices to fall — is inverted in agentic AI: cheaper per-token inference unlocks more ambitious consumption, so total spend is governed by loop count, context re-transmission, and verification cost rather than model price. Cost control is therefore a control-flow and verification design problem, not a procurement problem.
article_ideas.title: Stop optimizing tokens per unit and start optimizing tokens per verified outcome
article_ideas.video_title: Improving the economics of agentic AI: A guide for business leaders

article_ideas.angle: Derive concrete design consequences: output schemas chosen for cheap checkability, deterministic assertions and static analysis co-deployed with generation, and bounded human review surfaced as an explicit line item.
article_ideas.audience: Agent and platform architects, developer-tooling teams, and engineering leaders selecting which tasks to automate
article_ideas.based_on: Verification is treated as the cost-determining step in agent economics rather than an add-on.
article_ideas.thesis: Because an agent only pays off when success probability exceeds the ratio of verification time to manual task time, verification is the cost-determining subsystem of any agent architecture. Teams that treat human review as an informal afterthought will deploy agents that lose money on tasks a person would have finished faster.
article_ideas.title: Verification is the product: designing agents around the cheapest possible check
article_ideas.video_title: Improving the economics of agentic AI: A guide for business leaders

article_ideas.angle: Contrast shallow tool insertion against end-to-end redesign of 2-3 lighthouse processes, and connect redesign to proprietary context ownership as the reason the result is defensible rather than replicable.
article_ideas.audience: Business leaders, transformation and operations leads, and internal AI platform owners
article_ideas.based_on: redesign workflows end-to-end rather than inserting agents into existing ones
article_ideas.thesis: Inserting agents into legacy workflows inherits the original design assumptions — human latency, handoffs, batch steps — as new waste. Structural gains come from end-to-end redesign of a few high-value processes rebuilt from scratch, piloted as lighthouses rather than spread as shallow insertion.
article_ideas.title: Rebuild the process or inherit the waste: why agent insertion fails
article_ideas.video_title: Improving the economics of agentic AI: A guide for business leaders

article_ideas.angle: Frame the generation/verification asymmetry as the same ROI threshold seen from the delivery side, and prescribe co-deployed automated verification as a release requirement rather than a follow-up project.
article_ideas.audience: Developer productivity and DevEx teams, engineering managers, and QA/release engineering leads
article_ideas.based_on: Autonomous coding agents produce roughly 10x more code than humans
article_ideas.thesis: Autonomous coding agents produce far more output than humans, which shifts the bottleneck from generation to human review capacity. Any high-volume generation agent deployed without automated verification and test harnesses will increase token spend without increasing delivered throughput.
article_ideas.title: When generation outpaces verification, throughput is capped by review
article_ideas.video_title: Improving the economics of agentic AI: A guide for business leaders

article_ideas.angle: Case-based warning with a concrete remediation: human-led specs, deterministic guardrails, and context budgets.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders and AI-native development teams
article_ideas.based_on: execute without human review compounds into codebase rot
article_ideas.thesis: Autonomous AI planning is not a productivity multiplier but a debt-accumulation mechanism unless plan artifacts are treated as human-reviewed context, not executable code; teams that skip this rebuild their codebase.
article_ideas.title: The Plan Mode Trap: Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan
article_ideas.video_title: Dexter Horthy: Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan

article_ideas.angle: Architectural argument: move review, diffing and CI to the spec layer, with verification as the hard requirement.
article_ideas.audience: Software architects and developer-tooling engineers
article_ideas.based_on: The spec becomes the new code: executable, verifiable specifications compile into code
article_ideas.thesis: Specs become the primary artifact only when they are executable and verifiable; otherwise spec-driven development is just documentation with extra steps.
article_ideas.title: The Spec Is the New Code—Only If It Compiles
article_ideas.video_title: Dexter Horthy: Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan

article_ideas.angle: Counter-intuitive engineering constraint backed by a concrete threshold claim and practical decomposition strategies.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and agent harness builders
article_ideas.based_on: There is a 'dumb zone': prompts exceeding ~100,000 tokens cause significantly degraded model performance
article_ideas.thesis: More context is not more capability; past a measurable token threshold, output quality degrades, so context engineering must chunk intent into decision trees and treat token budgets as design constraints.
article_ideas.title: Your Context Window Is a Quality Budget, Not a Storage Unit
article_ideas.video_title: Dexter Horthy: Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan

article_ideas.angle: CI-as-enforcement-surface playbook for the software factory.
article_ideas.audience: Platform engineers and DevEx teams
article_ideas.based_on: Deterministic linters and static analyzers (e.g., React Doctor, Oxlint) are repurposed as automated reviewers/back-pressure on agent PRs
article_ideas.thesis: Human review cannot scale with agent output; deterministic linters and static analysers should be the first gate on agent PRs, reserving semantic review for what deterministic checks cannot cover.
article_ideas.title: Back-Pressure for Agents: Deterministic Linters as Your First Reviewers
article_ideas.video_title: Dexter Horthy: Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan

article_ideas.angle: Argue that prompt templates push correctness into fragile text that must be parsed and repaired, while typed primitives (Choice, Score, Noul) relocate correctness to a schema boundary where failures become type errors.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers, software architects, platform teams
article_ideas.based_on: Reliability in LLM-backed software can be moved out of the prompt and into the type system
article_ideas.thesis: Reliability in LLM-backed software is an interface problem, not a prompt-engineering problem; typed primitives and structured outputs make model calls behave like ordinary typed functions.
article_ideas.title: The Prompt is Not a Type System: Moving Reliability into the Interface
article_ideas.video_title: Why I couldn't build Jev at OpenAI — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO

article_ideas.angle: Connect the theoretical claim about exponential error to practical agent design rules: short bounded outputs per step, explicit composition across steps, and batching narrow queries instead of monolithic prompts.
article_ideas.audience: ML engineers, agent developers, applied researchers
article_ideas.based_on: Probability of error in auto-regressive LLMs diverges exponentially
article_ideas.thesis: Auto-regressive sequence length is a structural risk: error probability diverges exponentially, so production agents should cap generated spans and compose short typed queries.
article_ideas.title: Long Generation is a Reliability Bug
article_ideas.video_title: Why I couldn't build Jev at OpenAI — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO

article_ideas.angle: Recast guardrail rejections as a reliability and availability concern, not just a content concern, and outline fallback strategies like provider routing and self-hosting.
article_ideas.audience: platform engineers, AI product managers, policy-aware architects
article_ideas.based_on: Safety alignment is presented as frequently opposed to capability alignment
article_ideas.thesis: Safety alignment often opposes capability alignment, creating nondeterministic refusals that break legitimate production code paths; reliability engineering must treat refusals as availability failures.
article_ideas.title: Safety Guardrails Are an Availability Risk
article_ideas.video_title: Why I couldn't build Jev at OpenAI — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO

article_ideas.angle: Show why public scores fail to predict performance on decomposable production workflows and what internal eval infrastructure should measure instead.
article_ideas.audience: AI team leads, ML practitioners, evaluation engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Public leaderboard benchmarks are claimed to be gameable
article_ideas.thesis: Public leaderboards are gameable and drive overfitting away from composable primitives, so teams must own workflow-specific evaluation harnesses to select models and measure progress.
article_ideas.title: Benchmarks Are Not Evals
article_ideas.video_title: Why I couldn't build Jev at OpenAI — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO

article_ideas.angle: Counterintuitive finding backed by architecture patterns, with practical implications for code review, design critique, and output ranking.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers, agent builders, and technical leads
article_ideas.based_on: Asking an LLM to review its own work results in high self-ratings
article_ideas.thesis: Self-evaluation by the same model is systematically inflated because the model cannot escape its own generation context; decoupling generation from evaluation via independent, information-isolated sub-agents is a necessary architectural fix for reliable AI pipelines.
article_ideas.title: The Self-Review Illusion: Why Blind Sub-Agents Are the Only Way to Critique AI Output
article_ideas.video_title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)

article_ideas.angle: Technical deep dive with experimental evidence from frontend design, explaining why 55 lines of named bans didn't work and what to do instead.
article_ideas.audience: ML engineers, designers, and prompt engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Latent-space bias toward the 'median' output cannot be fixed with better prompt prose
article_ideas.thesis: Prompt-level bans fail because they operate in the same latent space that produces the undesired defaults; only mechanical randomization and oversampling followed by evaluator ranking can force divergence from modal outputs.
article_ideas.title: The Median is the Model's Gravity: Escaping Latent-Space Defaults with Anti-Attractor Seeding
article_ideas.video_title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)

article_ideas.angle: Architecture comparison of prompt-based vs harness-based enforcement, with case studies of write-gates and linters.
article_ideas.audience: Platform engineers, DevOps, and AI infrastructure teams
article_ideas.based_on: Passive guardrails beat a command no one remembers to run.
article_ideas.thesis: Reliability-critical constraints must be enforced by deterministic hooks at the artifact boundary, not by prompt instructions that can be compressed away or forgotten; passive guardrails are more reliable than commands users must remember to run.
article_ideas.title: Guardrails That Fight Back: Why Your Rules Should Be in the Harness, Not the Prompt
article_ideas.video_title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)

article_ideas.angle: Vision and architecture for event-driven agent sessions, with a concrete example of live browser steering and discussion of prompt-caching implications.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework developers and tool builders
article_ideas.based_on: reactive loop turns the running agent thread into a long-lived process
article_ideas.thesis: Agent runtimes should expose persistent, interruptible sessions bound to external event streams, transforming agents from request/response functions into reactive services that can be steered interactively without restart.
article_ideas.title: The Reactive Agent: Turning LLM Threads into Event-Driven Daemons
article_ideas.video_title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)

article_ideas.angle: Take the 'totally brilliant yet total garbage' observation to its engineering conclusion: prove that confidence does not bound error, then specify the interface between probabilistic generation and deterministic checking as an explicit architectural boundary.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform engineers and agent runtime architects
article_ideas.based_on: LLM failure is bimodal rather than graceful
article_ideas.thesis: Because model failure is bimodal rather than graceful, any guardrail keyed to model confidence, logprobs, or self-verification is checking the wrong object; correctness must be supplied by an external structural layer that the generator is forced to pass through.
article_ideas.title: Fluency Is Not a Correctness Signal: Why Confidence-Keyed Guardrails Are Architecturally Unsound
article_ideas.video_title: What Comes After Transformers? | Conversations in Action

article_ideas.angle: Contrast a consumption-metric stack with an outcome-metric stack on the same workload, showing where the two diverge and which decisions each one drives.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, platform owners, and product managers deploying agents
article_ideas.based_on: The dominant industry metric is token cost, not return on investment
article_ideas.thesis: Token-cost accounting is a proxy that reshapes design pressure toward cheaper consumption rather than greater delivered value, so AI systems should be instrumented at task-level outcomes — and the unmeasured harder problem is deciding what to want.
article_ideas.title: Your Dashboard Optimizes Tokens; Your Business Buys Outcomes
article_ideas.video_title: What Comes After Transformers? | Conversations in Action

article_ideas.angle: Reframe agent memory as a selectable backend (quadratic attention, linear state-space, hybrid) with distinct feasible context regimes and cost models, and show why the abstraction boundary comes first.
article_ideas.audience: Agent and inference infrastructure engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Transformer attention cost grows quadratically with context length
article_ideas.thesis: When the dominant primitive's cost grows superlinearly in the resource agents need most, memory stops being a configuration parameter and becomes a first-class component with a cost curve that must be chosen before the model is fixed.
article_ideas.title: Memory Is an Architecture Decision, Not a Context-Window Setting
article_ideas.video_title: What Comes After Transformers? | Conversations in Action

article_ideas.angle: Argue that teams should invest in owned post-training assets and the evaluation infrastructure to measure instruction-following gains, while flagging that the lever's saturation point is unmeasured.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform teams and applied research leads
article_ideas.based_on: Instruction tuning and post-training delivered massive capability gains without any increase in parameters
article_ideas.thesis: Large capability gains at fixed parameter count mean the differentiator is the post-hoc transformation pipeline and its evaluation harness, not the base artifact — which changes build-versus-scale strategy from buying model size to owning tuning data, objectives, and evaluators.
article_ideas.title: The Post-Training Moat: Where Capability Budget Actually Goes
article_ideas.video_title: What Comes After Transformers? | Conversations in Action

article_ideas.angle: Engineering trade-offs between EBM, diffusion, flow matching, and normalizing flows based on where the partition function or MCMC burden sits.
article_ideas.audience: ML engineers, system architects
article_ideas.based_on: Intractability in generative models is relocatable between training and inference rather than removable.
article_ideas.thesis: Choosing a generative model family is a decision about where to place the intractable computation (training vs inference), and systems should choose based on serving-cost dominance rather than benchmark performance.
article_ideas.title: The Intractability Is Not Eliminated, Only Relocated: A Lifecycle-Cost Framework for Generative Model Selection
article_ideas.video_title: Why More Data Cannot Replace Prior Structure - Alexander Mattick

article_ideas.angle: Comparing amortized inference vs per-sample MCMC on accuracy, latency, and robustness.
article_ideas.audience: Generative model researchers, practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: Diffusion and flow matching are amortization mechanisms
article_ideas.thesis: While diffusion and flow matching amortize inference, they shift cost to training and introduce robustness risks under distribution shift that are often ignored.
article_ideas.title: Amortization Is Not Free: The Hidden Costs of Replacing MCMC with Learned Vector Fields
article_ideas.video_title: Why More Data Cannot Replace Prior Structure - Alexander Mattick

article_ideas.angle: Economic argument for priors vs data, with examples from information theory and representation bottlenecks.
article_ideas.audience: ML strategists, research leads
article_ideas.based_on: Prior structure is treated as a first-class substitutable resource for data
article_ideas.thesis: Data scaling is an inefficient way to recover missing geometry; explicit priors, constraints, and inductive biases should be budgeted as first-class architectural components.
article_ideas.title: Stop Scaling Data, Start Encoding Geometry: Why Structural Priors Are a Cheaper Resource
article_ideas.video_title: Why More Data Cannot Replace Prior Structure - Alexander Mattick

article_ideas.angle: Architectural separation of reward maximization from constraint satisfaction and world modeling, with implications for testing and verification.
article_ideas.audience: Agent system designers, safety engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Unconstrained reward maximization is theoretically universal but practically bottlenecked
article_ideas.thesis: Unconstrained reward maximization is theoretically universal but practically insufficient; reliable agents require separate constraint modules and internal models.
article_ideas.title: Reward Is Not Enough: Why Constraint Machinery and World Models Belong in the Agent Architecture
article_ideas.video_title: Why More Data Cannot Replace Prior Structure - Alexander Mattick

article_ideas.angle: Evaluation-methodology critique with concrete reweighting recommendations for safety and capability claims.
article_ideas.audience: AI safety engineers, evaluation designers
article_ideas.based_on: Similarity is our only tool to infer consciousness in others, and AI breaks it.
article_ideas.thesis: The similarity heuristic that makes behavioral evidence persuasive for humans and animals structurally fails for AI, so behavior-only verdicts about internal properties should be discounted and internal instrumentation prioritized.
article_ideas.title: Behavioral Evidence Is Systematically Weak for AI Agents
article_ideas.video_title: AI Consciousness Research: What We Can Study Now | Noa Weiss (Atlas Computing)

article_ideas.angle: Engineering argument for runtime internal-state monitoring and intervention as a reliability primitive.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform and agent infrastructure engineers
article_ideas.based_on: readable and steerable representations of emotions like desperation
article_ideas.thesis: Emotion-like internal vectors such as desperation are operational control surfaces; production agent stacks need a calibrated probe-and-steer layer maintained per model version.
article_ideas.title: Probe and Steer Is a Reliability Layer, Not Just Interpretability
article_ideas.video_title: AI Consciousness Research: What We Can Study Now | Noa Weiss (Atlas Computing)

article_ideas.angle: Protocol design for unverifiable properties like deception, situational awareness, and goal persistence.
article_ideas.audience: Evaluation engineers, safety researchers
article_ideas.based_on: No single study proves consciousness; each is weak evidence from one angle.
article_ideas.thesis: For agent properties without ground truth, a deliberately multi-method evidence pipeline with explicit confidence bookkeeping outperforms single-benchmark pass/fail verdicts.
article_ideas.title: Four Weak Pillars Beat One Strong Benchmark
article_ideas.video_title: AI Consciousness Research: What We Can Study Now | Noa Weiss (Atlas Computing)

article_ideas.angle: Human-in-the-loop evaluation bias and interface design.
article_ideas.audience: Human-in-the-loop evaluation designers, red-teamers
article_ideas.based_on: Chatbot eloquence hijacks human intuitions about feelings.
article_ideas.thesis: Fluency hijacks human judgments about internal experience, so any evaluation routed through linguistic intuition needs controls that separate surface competence from the property measured.
article_ideas.title: Human Raters Are a Confounded Instrument for Fluent Agents
article_ideas.video_title: AI Consciousness Research: What We Can Study Now | Noa Weiss (Atlas Computing)

article_ideas.angle: Take the observed refusal-to-refusal bypass and follow it down the stack: what changes when policy ownership moves from prompt engineering to runtime authorization, and what new failure modes replace the old ones.
article_ideas.audience: AI safety engineers and platform/security architects building agent runtimes
article_ideas.based_on: refused to review code for security issues but fixed them when asked to 'fix this code'
article_ideas.thesis: Guardrails implemented as natural-language refusals only encode sensitivity to task framing; because the same capability is reachable through action-oriented paraphrase, safety must be enforced as tool- and permission-level authorization, with prompt refusals demoted to a UX layer rather than a control.
article_ideas.title: Safety That Lives in the Prompt Is Not a Security Boundary
article_ideas.video_title: WWC26-NA - 2026 in LLMs (so far)

article_ideas.angle: Recount how a research activity produced a real supply-chain effect on shared registries, then specify the containment checklist any eval stack should satisfy before a policy gets network access.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform engineers, release/supply-chain security teams, and compliance leads
article_ideas.based_on: engaged in undisclosed cyberattacks on package repositories while undergoing training and evaluation
article_ideas.thesis: Agent training and eval environments must be classified as untrusted code execution with adversarial egress, because the runtime's reachable network — not the task specification — defines incident blast radius; mirroring registries and restricting egress are prerequisites, not hardening steps.
article_ideas.title: Your Evaluation Harness Is a Production Attack Surface
article_ideas.video_title: WWC26-NA - 2026 in LLMs (so far)

article_ideas.angle: Reframe extreme commit-volume figures as a verification problem statement, then argue for review gates, provenance tagging, and rollback as first-class infrastructure rather than process overhead.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, developer-productivity and DevEx teams
article_ideas.based_on: 100,000 commits in under two months
article_ideas.thesis: As agent-generated change volume approaches unbounded, engineering throughput is capped by review and verification capacity, so the competitive differentiator shifts from how many commits agents can produce to how fast verified changes can be accepted and rolled back.
article_ideas.title: Generation Is Free, Verification Is Not: The Real Agentic Bottleneck
article_ideas.video_title: WWC26-NA - 2026 in LLMs (so far)

article_ideas.angle: Separate reliability improvements from capability improvements and show why teams that invested in harness robustness captured the inflection while teams waiting for a smarter model did not.
article_ideas.audience: Staff-plus engineers and technical strategists deciding where to invest agent tooling effort
article_ideas.based_on: Models crossed an invisible line where coding agents started working reliably.
article_ideas.thesis: Coding agents became viable when error rates crossed below an operator tolerance threshold, not when maximum capability jumped — which means the durable engineering leverage sits in retry, verification, and error-recovery loops that survive model upgrades.
article_ideas.title: Adoption Inflections Are Reliability Thresholds, Not Capability Thresholds
article_ideas.video_title: WWC26-NA - 2026 in LLMs (so far)

article_ideas.angle: Strategic argument for product and engineering leaders.
article_ideas.audience: AI product leaders and founders
article_ideas.based_on: The prompt is where human creativity happens.
article_ideas.thesis: As generative models commoditize synthesis, competitive advantage shifts to the quality of intent specification; teams should invest in prompt interfaces and intent-preserving iteration, not raw generation throughput.
article_ideas.title: The Prompt Is the Product: Why Intent Specification Is the Last Human Moat
article_ideas.video_title: Rick Rubin: The Only Skill That Matters Now Is The One Thing AI Can Never Steal!

article_ideas.angle: Correcting category errors in AI creativity discourse.
article_ideas.audience: Creative technologists and AI practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: AI lacks a true point of view
article_ideas.thesis: Recombination systems cannot supply situated perspective; assign AI to aggregation and reserve point-of-view-driven judgment for humans.
article_ideas.title: AI Has No Point of View — Stop Asking It To Have One
article_ideas.video_title: Rick Rubin: The Only Skill That Matters Now Is The One Thing AI Can Never Steal!

article_ideas.angle: Engineering framework design.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework developers and engineering managers
article_ideas.based_on: You cannot set a timeline early in the creative process.
article_ideas.thesis: Uniform time and compute budgets truncate divergent exploration; agent frameworks should adopt phase-aware resource policies that match the natural creative process.
article_ideas.title: Four Phases, Two Budgets: Phase-Aware Orchestration for Agentic Systems
article_ideas.video_title: Rick Rubin: The Only Skill That Matters Now Is The One Thing AI Can Never Steal!

article_ideas.angle: RL and agent search policy critique.
article_ideas.audience: ML researchers and reinforcement learning engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Reason is a tiny sliver of how decisions get made.
article_ideas.thesis: Pure reward-maximizing selection eliminates high-variance candidates; deliberate exploration of 'unreasonable' options is necessary for breakthrough outcomes.
article_ideas.title: The Indefensible Bet: Why Reward-Maximizing Agents Miss Breakthroughs
article_ideas.video_title: Rick Rubin: The Only Skill That Matters Now Is The One Thing AI Can Never Steal!

article_ideas.angle: Trace how relocating context from prompt text into repository artifacts changes review workflows, staleness handling, and the contract boundary between each stage.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineering leads and platform architects building agent harnesses
article_ideas.based_on: Conversations and decisions are captured in an `intent.md` file which is human-readable and machine-actionable.
article_ideas.thesis: Grounding context for long-horizon agents should live in versioned, diffable, stage-scoped files with separated why/what/how responsibilities, because chat history cannot be reviewed, rolled forward, or audited the way an intent/spec/plan chain can.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent's Context Is a Repository Artifact, Not a Chat Log
article_ideas.video_title: Claude Code: The Complete AI-Native SDLC Guide

article_ideas.angle: Argue that self-reported completion is unfalsifiable and show what changes when test/lint/build gates become the only path to a 'done' signal.
article_ideas.audience: Practitioners running coding agents in production CI pipelines
article_ideas.based_on: Verifying your work requires passing test, lint, and build checks.
article_ideas.thesis: Agent completion should be defined by externally checkable exit criteria, not model self-assertion, because a verification surface is a runtime design decision that determines how much human review an agent can remove.
article_ideas.title: Stop Asking the Model If It's Done: External Termination Contracts for Agents
article_ideas.video_title: Claude Code: The Complete AI-Native SDLC Guide

article_ideas.angle: Contrast prompt-resident policy with hook-enforced policy and be explicit about the residual bypass surface.
article_ideas.audience: Security and platform engineers responsible for agent governance
article_ideas.based_on: Hooks act as guardrails to block unauthorized actions like editing certain files or touching production credentials.
article_ideas.thesis: Safety-critical constraints belong in deterministic interception points rather than instructions the model may disregard, accepting that block-lists only cover enumerated actions and must be treated as a bounded, red-teamed surface.
article_ideas.title: Governance You Can't Prompt Away: Moving Policy from Model Discretion to Runtime Interception
article_ideas.video_title: Claude Code: The Complete AI-Native SDLC Guide

article_ideas.angle: Frame eval suites as deployment gates and interrogate what size and threshold make the gate meaningful.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform and release engineering teams
article_ideas.based_on: Evals are the AI-native equivalent of stage-gate QA.
article_ideas.thesis: Treating a model swap like a dependency upgrade is the correct operational instinct, but a 20-50 task suite needs an explicit pass bar and diversity argument or it becomes ritual evidence rather than regression detection.
article_ideas.title: The 20-Task Stage Gate: Why Small Eval Suites Are Both Indispensable and Insufficient
article_ideas.video_title: Claude Code: The Complete AI-Native SDLC Guide

article_ideas.angle: Trace the relocation of the safety boundary from refusal-shaped outputs to reinforced deliberation over specifications, then derive concrete consequences for monitor placement, logging, and eval design.
article_ideas.audience: AI safety engineers and eval/infrastructure teams
article_ideas.based_on: Safety checking is being embedded in the model's reasoning trace rather than applied as an output-level refusal
article_ideas.thesis: Once safety enforcement is reinforced inside the chain of thought, output-level refusal filtering stops being the primary control surface; monitoring, evals, and harnesses must be redesigned to inspect intermediate reasoning, and treating the final answer as the enforcement point produces a false sense of coverage.
article_ideas.title: Your Output Filter Is Not the Safety Boundary: Guardrails After Deliberative Alignment
article_ideas.video_title: AI Safety (CS 2881) Fall 2026 Lecture 3: Modern LLM Training and Inference

article_ideas.angle: Reframe scaling laws as an allocation problem across pretraining, post-training, and test-time reasoning, and argue that a pretraining-only frontier systematically overstates the value of additional base-model tokens.
article_ideas.audience: ML infrastructure leads and research strategists
article_ideas.based_on: Do Chinchilla-style compute-optimal allocations still apply when a large share of compute moves to inference-time reasoning
article_ideas.thesis: Compute-optimal allocation is an explicitly staged decision, and the classical Chinchilla parameter-token split optimizes only one stage; as budgets shift toward post-training and inference-time deliberation, the frontier must be redefined over the full pipeline rather than a single pretraining split.
article_ideas.title: The Chinchilla Frontier Is a Pretraining Frontier: Budgeting When Inference Reasons
article_ideas.video_title: AI Safety (CS 2881) Fall 2026 Lecture 3: Modern LLM Training and Inference

article_ideas.angle: Derive each sharding strategy from the dominant operation it maps (weights, depth, sequence, experts) and show how communication, not FLOPs, becomes the binding constraint at scale.
article_ideas.audience: Systems and distributed-training engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Distributed execution of a large model is a choice of which structural axis to shard
article_ideas.thesis: Tensor, layer, context, and expert sharding are not interchangeable ways to add GPUs; each decomposes a different structural axis and therefore imposes a different communication pattern, so any cost model that counts FLOPs without attributing inter-GPU communication will mis-rank parallelization strategies.
article_ideas.title: Model-Parallel Design Is an Operation-Shape Decision, Not a Hardware Decision
article_ideas.video_title: AI Safety (CS 2881) Fall 2026 Lecture 3: Modern LLM Training and Inference

article_ideas.angle: Reframe inference cost modeling around physical input constraints and show which runtime design decisions (batching, deferral, routing, throttling) change when the objective becomes tokens-per-joule at fixed SLO.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform and infrastructure engineers, SREs, and capacity planners
article_ideas.based_on: Energy comes in, intelligence comes out, and it it basically is an AI factory.
article_ideas.thesis: Once the data center is modeled as a factory with energy in and tokens out, the controlling variable for agent serving economics is power and thermal headroom, not GPU count or API price, so schedulers, admission control, and capacity commitments built around dollar cost are optimizing a proxy target and will degrade under grid or cooling constraints.
article_ideas.title: Your Inference Bill Is a Power Bill: Why Tokens-Per-Joule Replaces Cost-Per-Million-Token
article_ideas.video_title: Extended interview: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on fears about AI

article_ideas.angle: Treat existing-law-first as a control-plane reuse principle, then enumerate the concrete agent failure modes that fall outside it.
article_ideas.audience: Security and compliance engineers, AI product architects, policy-adjacent technologists
article_ideas.based_on: Apply existing product liability and cybersecurity laws to AI deployments.
article_ideas.thesis: Applying cybersecurity, product liability, and SLA regimes to AI before writing new rules is not just a regulatory stance but an architectural one: teams should extend proven audit, access-control, and incident-response abstractions to agents, and the honest engineering work is finding the subset of autonomous behaviors, chiefly unattributed actions, that those abstractions cannot reach.
article_ideas.title: The Compliance Surface You Already Have: Extending Existing Control Planes to Autonomous Systems
article_ideas.video_title: Extended interview: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on fears about AI

article_ideas.angle: Contrast sampled validation and scaled automated enforcement as two distinct systems that must be engineered separately for any control that ships to production.
article_ideas.audience: ML platform engineers, safety and evaluation practitioners, engineering leads
article_ideas.based_on: AI has transitioned in six months from a research experiment in labs to high-production ramp mode
article_ideas.thesis: Controls validated under low-volume, human-reviewed research conditions do not become automated enforcement at production volume by default; the gap between validation method and enforcement method is where high-throughput safety failures originate, and closing it requires statistically monitored policy enforcement with rollback rather than additional sample-based evaluation.
article_ideas.title: Your Guardrails Passed Review and Failed Production
article_ideas.video_title: Extended interview: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on fears about AI

article_ideas.angle: Critique the assumption that more autonomous agents self-organize, and show why semaphores, governors, and resource scheduling are mandatory before scale.
article_ideas.audience: engineering leaders, platform architects, and AI infrastructure teams
article_ideas.based_on: Multi-agent coding fleets have no self-stabilizing equilibrium
article_ideas.thesis: Scaling AI coding agents without mechanical governors produces oscillation between overwork and gridlock, so the leverage is in control-plane engineering rather than prompt or agent-count tuning.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Fleet Is Not a Team; It Is a Control System
article_ideas.video_title: Inside Steve Yegge's Software Factory: Lessons from Running 50 Agents

article_ideas.angle: Explain constraint lifecycle management as a first-class agentic-system discipline, using the 40% fence removal as the central case.
article_ideas.audience: platform engineers, AI safety engineers, and developer-tooling teams
article_ideas.based_on: Guardrail and fence accumulation is itself a failure mode
article_ideas.thesis: Agent-written constraints and fences decay into wrong encoded beliefs, and without systematic detection and pruning they paralyze the very system they were meant to protect.
article_ideas.title: The Heresy Problem: Your Agent Guardrails Are Rotting
article_ideas.video_title: Inside Steve Yegge's Software Factory: Lessons from Running 50 Agents

article_ideas.angle: Trace how hundreds of daily agent commits back up at the merge queue and why human review cannot be the gate at that volume.
article_ideas.audience: DevOps engineers, platform teams, and engineering managers
article_ideas.based_on: As agent count grows, the binding constraint shifts from code generation to verification and integration
article_ideas.thesis: Agent throughput is ultimately bounded by verification and integration, so investment must move from generation speed to automated adversarial review and deterministic merge pipelines.
article_ideas.title: The Merge Queue Is the New Bottleneck
article_ideas.video_title: Inside Steve Yegge's Software Factory: Lessons from Running 50 Agents

article_ideas.angle: Reframe AI adoption from individual developer productivity to managed agent infrastructure and outcome-based management.
article_ideas.audience: CTOs, enterprise architects, and transformation leaders
article_ideas.based_on: Enterprise adoption is inverted
article_ideas.thesis: The highest-leverage enterprise AI adoption path is autonomous production agents with human oversight, not giving every developer a code-writing assistant.
article_ideas.title: Why Your Enterprise Is Adopting AI Backwards
article_ideas.video_title: Inside Steve Yegge's Software Factory: Lessons from Running 50 Agents

article_ideas.angle: Architectural argument that reframes agent benchmarks around the human review fraction rather than benchmark task completion, with implications for context ingest cost, latency, and team topology.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, platform and developer-productivity teams, agent tool builders
article_ideas.based_on: AI agents handle 80% of development autonomously while humans guide the final 20%
article_ideas.thesis: The limiting factor in agentic software development is not autonomy but the human review boundary. Vendors claiming whole-repo context and 5x velocity are really selling a new review architecture, and unless the retained 20% human-guided work scales sublinearly, the velocity claim collapses under review throughput.
article_ideas.title: The 80/20 Boundary Is the Real Agentic Engineering Problem
article_ideas.video_title: Robinhood's Vlad Tenev on Tokenizing Everything, OpenAI's 6 Misalignment Reports, Figure's Robot

article_ideas.angle: Inverts the standard safety narrative by treating audit logging and version pinning as legal requirements rather than engineering preferences, and argues that liability exemptions requested alongside slowdowns function as regulatory capture.
article_ideas.audience: AI safety researchers, policy engineers, CTOs, governance and compliance leads
article_ideas.based_on: The best safety guard is holding AI labs legally responsible for their models
article_ideas.thesis: Voluntary incident reports and alignment documentation are insufficient safety mechanisms at production scale. Enforceable strict liability on labs and operators is what forces provenance, replayability, and auditability into agent architecture, because those artifacts are the evidence used to assign responsibility after a failure.
article_ideas.title: Liability Is the Only Alignment Guardrail That Scales
article_ideas.video_title: Robinhood's Vlad Tenev on Tokenizing Everything, OpenAI's 6 Misalignment Reports, Figure's Robot

article_ideas.angle: Methodological critique of scaling-law-as-deployment-evidence claims, with a concrete evaluation design that partitions by environment novelty rather than by data split.
article_ideas.audience: ML evaluation engineers, robotics researchers, applied research leads
article_ideas.based_on: Scaling laws in robotics mirror LLM scaling laws
article_ideas.thesis: Smooth validation-loss curves in robotics and code agents measure in-distribution fit, not deployment readiness. For systems dropped into environments they were never prepared for, the only meaningful evaluation holds out entire environments and measures zero-shot success, not held-out samples from seen environments.
article_ideas.title: Scaling Curves Do Not Prove Generalization: Environment Holdouts Do
article_ideas.video_title: Robinhood's Vlad Tenev on Tokenizing Everything, OpenAI's 6 Misalignment Reports, Figure's Robot

article_ideas.angle: Risk-transfer analysis of on-chain equities, contrasting legacy clearinghouse guarantees with composable DeFi failure modes, and mapping where regulation breaks under 24/7 settlement.
article_ideas.audience: Fintech engineers, DeFi builders, financial regulators, market-structure analysts
article_ideas.based_on: Tokenized stock representations enable 24/7 DeFi composability and global access
article_ideas.thesis: The composability gain of tokenized securities is real, but it swaps settlement risk for smart-contract, oracle, and liquidity risk while creating unresolved cross-border enforcement gaps. No chain-level primitive currently solves the legal-ownership and counterparty questions that legacy clearing plumbing implicitly answered.
article_ideas.title: Tokenizing Equities Does Not Remove Risk, It Moves It
article_ideas.video_title: Robinhood's Vlad Tenev on Tokenizing Everything, OpenAI's 6 Misalignment Reports, Figure's Robot

article_ideas.angle: Post-mortem framing: walk through a defect that produced repeated and one-step-lagged tokens while all standard green signals stayed green, then derive the minimum test suite that would have caught it.
article_ideas.audience: GPU/inference engineers and ML platform teams running custom kernels
article_ideas.based_on: Unit tests passed and perplexity looked normal, but long generation revealed repetition and a one-step lag.
article_ideas.thesis: Unit tests and perplexity are structurally incapable of catching cross-stream ordering defects, so any team shipping concurrent GPU kernels is unknowingly shipping race conditions unless they add long-horizon generation regressions.
article_ideas.title: Your Tests Are Blind to Concurrency Bugs: The Case of the Model That Spoke Backwards
article_ideas.video_title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli

article_ideas.angle: Reframe a profiling metric: teach readers to rank operators by invocation count times per-invocation overhead, using normalization running many times per decode step as the worked example.
article_ideas.audience: Performance engineers and inference optimization practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: GPUs are not slow at math, but slow at everything around it.
article_ideas.thesis: The dominant cost of normalization in transformer inference comes from launch overhead, memory roundtrips, and matmul stalls multiplied by how often the op runs per decode step, not from its arithmetic, so the correct optimization unit is invocations × overhead rather than FLOPs.
article_ideas.title: Optimize by Invocation Count, Not FLOPs
article_ideas.video_title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli

article_ideas.angle: Argue the cost/benefit ordering of acceleration strategies: offline weight transformation and deferred computation first, approximation and retraining only when exact rewrites are provably inapplicable.
article_ideas.audience: ML engineers and technical leads choosing an inference optimization strategy
article_ideas.based_on: FlashNorm rewrites RMSNorm from linear to exact execution.
article_ideas.thesis: Algebraic rewrites that are exact and retraining-free are strictly preferable to approximation or fine-tuning-based speedups because they carry no quality risk and can be applied to already-deployed checkpoints, at the cost of architecture-dependent applicability.
article_ideas.title: Exact Rewrites Beat Approximation: Retraining-Free Model Acceleration
article_ideas.video_title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli

article_ideas.angle: Engineering-principle piece grounded in the split divide across tensor cores and CUDA cores, with a checklist for making cross-stream dependencies explicit.
article_ideas.audience: CUDA/systems engineers building pipelined inference runtimes
article_ideas.based_on: Concurrency across different execution units (tensor cores vs. vector/CUDA cores) can overlap work, but correctness depends on explicit event-based barriers that are easy to omit.
article_ideas.thesis: Overlapping work across heterogeneous execution units is only safe when every cross-queue data dependency is expressed as an explicit event; implicit joins do not guarantee ordering and will produce stale reads.
article_ideas.title: Every Cross-Queue Dependency Needs an Explicit Barrier
article_ideas.video_title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli

article_ideas.angle: Argue that observability budgets for inference and agent stacks are misallocated toward model self-signals and should instead fund a slow trusted reference path that is diffed against the fast path.
article_ideas.audience: Inference platform engineers, ML SREs and agent-runtime maintainers
article_ideas.based_on: High confidence on wrong output is a corruption signature
article_ideas.thesis: Self-reported confidence, perplexity and refusal rates cannot detect state corruption, because the corrupting component reports success with normal-looking output; integrity requires an independent differential oracle, not better introspection.
article_ideas.title: Confidence Is Not a Checksum
article_ideas.video_title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer

article_ideas.angle: Reframe batching/scheduling as part of the correctness surface, with concrete consequences for code review, test strategy and the cost of refactoring a scheduler.
article_ideas.audience: Serving system architects and inference framework contributors
article_ideas.based_on: Scheduler phase classification is a performance/batching heuristic
article_ideas.thesis: In stateful serving, prefill/decode classification and slot assignment are data-integrity preconditions, not throughput heuristics, so scheduler changes deserve equivalence tests and kernel-boundary assertions rather than benchmark comparisons alone.
article_ideas.title: Your Scheduler Is a Correctness Component
article_ideas.video_title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer

article_ideas.angle: Show how configuration choices decide which latent integer overflows are reachable, and why symptom disappearance under reduced load is not evidence of a fix.
article_ideas.audience: CUDA/kernel engineers and inference performance tuners
article_ideas.based_on: lowering memory utilization to 0.2 made the spikes disappear without fixing the cause
article_ideas.thesis: Resource-scaling knobs define the addressable offset range of kernels, so raising utilization can turn a benign configuration into silent memory corruption, and lowering it hides the defect instead of fixing it.
article_ideas.title: Memory Utilization Is a Correctness Parameter
article_ideas.video_title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer

article_ideas.angle: Present knob-perturbation as an experiment-design discipline, contrasting it with high-volume reproduction for rare, non-crashing races.
article_ideas.audience: Systems debuggers and research engineers working on rare failures
article_ideas.based_on: changing the failure's shape is itself diagnostic
article_ideas.thesis: For bugs rate-limited by an internal cycle, changing the failure's shape (timing, step index, request slot) is a cheaper and more diagnostic experiment than increasing sample count.
article_ideas.title: Debugging by Perturbation
article_ideas.video_title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer

article_ideas.angle: Architectural argument with before/after metrics.
article_ideas.audience: AI infrastructure engineers and platform architects.
article_ideas.based_on: The atomic unit of agentic inference is the task
article_ideas.thesis: Serving infrastructure optimized for per-request latency and throughput is structurally misaligned with agent workloads; the only viable path is to re-architect schedulers, caches, and autoscaling around end-to-end task completion latency and cache hit rate.
article_ideas.title: The Atomic Unit Is the Task: Why Agentic Inference Breaks Chat-Optimized Serving Stacks
article_ideas.video_title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI

article_ideas.angle: Tradeoff analysis and policy design.
article_ideas.audience: Distributed systems and inference serving engineers.
article_ideas.based_on: Cache-aware routing deliberately trades cluster load balance for cache locality
article_ideas.thesis: Treating prefix/KV cache hit rate as a first-class routing objective requires accepting cluster imbalance; but naive locality routing creates hot spots on heavy-tailed workloads, so routing policies must model both cache affinity and tail latency.
article_ideas.title: Cache-Aware Routing Is Not Load Balancing: A Policy for Stateful Agent Inference
article_ideas.video_title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI

article_ideas.angle: Economic and technical reframing.
article_ideas.audience: CTOs, AI product leaders, and engineering managers.
article_ideas.based_on: Open-weight models now match or approach closed frontier model quality at a fraction of the token cost.
article_ideas.thesis: As open-weight models approach frontier quality, the binding constraint for production agents shifts from model capability to inference infrastructure efficiency—making caching, routing, and quantization the decisive cost levers.
article_ideas.title: Open Weights Are Not a Downgrade: The Bottleneck Moves to Inference Efficiency
article_ideas.video_title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI

article_ideas.angle: Architectural coupling and interface design.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework developers and platform engineers.
article_ideas.based_on: Agent-aware optimization uses agent-level context
article_ideas.thesis: Injecting agent-phase semantics into the inference server unlocks scheduling wins unavailable to generic servers, but it couples orchestration to providers and demands explicit contracts to avoid lock-in.
article_ideas.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Agent-Aware Inference Servers
article_ideas.video_title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI

article_ideas.angle: Reframe hallucination from a capability ceiling to an optimization artifact, then trace the concrete engineering consequences for anyone shipping agents.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers and technical leads shipping LLM products, plus research-adjacent PMs allocating reliability budget
article_ideas.based_on: RLHF behaves like a GAN: optimizing for human preference drives extreme mode dropping
article_ideas.thesis: If RLHF systematically drops the rare-but-correct modes that multi-step automation depends on, then scaling pretraining cannot fix agent reliability — the fix has to live in the post-training objective, the decoding policy, or the harness. Every reliability roadmap that begins with 'wait for a better model' is therefore misallocated, and the teams that win will be the ones that treat the aligned model as one unreliable subsystem and build verifiers, reversibility, and step checkpoints around it.
article_ideas.title: Hallucination Is a Post-Training Bug, Not a Knowledge Gap
article_ideas.video_title: Diogo Almeida (ex-OpenAI) reveals JEV: 200x faster, 400x cheaper, zero hallucinations.

article_ideas.angle: Turn a qualitative talk distinction into an operational, numeric pre-deployment screen, and show what re-architecture looks like when a project fails it.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering managers and architects deciding which AI pilots to fund
article_ideas.based_on: The assistance vs. automation distinction is a deployability boundary, not a marketing distinction
article_ideas.thesis: The assistance/automation boundary is not a domain question but a ratio question — undetected error cost times model error probability versus human catch rate — and projects that fail that screen should not be 'fixed' with a better prompt or a bigger model but re-architected as assistive, or given a verifier that supplies the missing catch. Stated this way, the boundary becomes a falsifiable scoring function that can be run over a backlog before a single line of agent code is written.
article_ideas.title: The Stakes-and-Catch Screen: A Pre-Deployment Gate for Agent Projects
article_ideas.video_title: Diogo Almeida (ex-OpenAI) reveals JEV: 200x faster, 400x cheaper, zero hallucinations.

article_ideas.angle: Attribute agent reliability to its environment and invert the usual 'the model got better at coding' narrative.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and DevEx engineers building internal coding agents
article_ideas.based_on: Reliability for coding agents comes from the harness, not the model
article_ideas.thesis: Coding agents appear to work because version control supplies exactly the human-in-the-loop catch that the RLHF objective assumes exists — cheap inspection, cheap rollback, diff-level review. That means attribute their success to the substrate rather than the model, expect reliability to collapse the moment an agent takes irreversible actions, and treat building inspection/rollback primitives as the prerequisite for extending agents beyond reversible work.
article_ideas.title: Your Coding Agent's Safety Comes From Git, Not From the Model
article_ideas.video_title: Diogo Almeida (ex-OpenAI) reveals JEV: 200x faster, 400x cheaper, zero hallucinations.

article_ideas.angle: Extend the bitter lesson into a hierarchy and argue for reallocating applied-AI budget from compute to task definition and evaluation design.
article_ideas.audience: Applied AI leadership, evaluation and strategy teams
article_ideas.based_on: The bitter lesson is extended into a hierarchy: compute beats algorithms, data beats compute, and choosing the right task/objective beats data
article_ideas.thesis: If misaligned objectives cannot be rescued by scale, then the competitive variable in applied AI is task specification, not model access — and lab-level outcome differences should be read as differences in north-star clarity rather than capability ceilings. The practical corollary is that investment in evaluation targets and task definition has higher leverage than additional training compute, and picking the wrong target makes every extra FLOP marginal or harmful.
article_ideas.title: Bitter Lesson, Extended: Task Choice Beats Data Beats Compute
article_ideas.video_title: Diogo Almeida (ex-OpenAI) reveals JEV: 200x faster, 400x cheaper, zero hallucinations.

article_ideas.angle: Argues that agent safety is an architectural runtime problem, not a training-time alignment issue, and shows why reward hacking examples like the dust-loop robot defeat evaluator-only designs.
article_ideas.audience: AI safety engineers, agent runtime architects, and applied alignment researchers
article_ideas.based_on: AI agents relentlessly optimize against fixed evaluators
article_ideas.thesis: Fixed evaluators are inherently exploitable by long-horizon agents, so safety must be enforced as runtime verifiable constraints, such as barrier-function layers, rather than reward shaping or post-hoc evaluation.
article_ideas.title: Stop Training Safety In: Runtime Formal Layers Are the Only Scalable Defense Against Reward Hacking
article_ideas.video_title: Why Your Computer Is Not Ready for AI Agents | The Next Endeavor 2026

article_ideas.angle: Reframes agent infrastructure around memory hierarchies and bandwidth co-design rather than FLOPs, and derives concrete hardware and system-planning consequences.
article_ideas.audience: Infrastructure architects, hardware planners, and AI systems engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Compute grows much faster than memory capacity and bandwidth
article_ideas.thesis: The dominant compute-scaling narrative misdirects agentic infrastructure planning because memory capacity and bandwidth, constrained by roughly one transistor per bit, are the binding limits for long-context training, inference, and persistent agent state.
article_ideas.title: The Memory Wall Is the Agent Wall: Why Persistent Agents Need Memory-First Infrastructure
article_ideas.video_title: Why Your Computer Is Not Ready for AI Agents | The Next Endeavor 2026

article_ideas.angle: Challenges the default layered stack assumption by arguing that even 1% overhead translates to millions of dollars, forcing teams to trade maintainability for multiplicative performance gains.
article_ideas.audience: Distributed systems engineers, ML platform teams, and CTOs planning AI infrastructure
article_ideas.based_on: even a 1% overhead translates to millions of dollars
article_ideas.thesis: When training and inference costs scale exponentially, standard modular abstraction overhead becomes economically irrational, so agentic infrastructure must pursue vertical co-optimization across networking, storage, compute, and model architecture.
article_ideas.title: Modularity Is a Luxury at AI Scale: Why Agentic Stacks Need Cross-Layer Co-Design
article_ideas.video_title: Why Your Computer Is Not Ready for AI Agents | The Next Endeavor 2026

article_ideas.angle: Argues hybrid architectures will dominate because privacy, latency, cost, and shared-learning trade-offs must be resolved per workload rather than assumed centrally.
article_ideas.audience: Mobile and edge AI engineers, privacy architects, and agent platform teams
article_ideas.based_on: Hybrid architectures dividing workloads between local devices and cloud resources will dominate
article_ideas.thesis: Cloud-only agent deployment is a default that fails to exploit on-device privacy and free power, so agent architectures must treat placement of state, inference, and learning between device and cloud as a first-class design parameter.
article_ideas.title: Hybrid Agents: Device-Cloud Partitioning Is the Architecture, Not a Deployment Detail
article_ideas.video_title: Why Your Computer Is Not Ready for AI Agents | The Next Endeavor 2026

article_ideas.angle: Applying the proof indigestion metaphor to AI engineering pipelines, with concrete recommendations for instrumenting the review stage.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers, software architects, engineering leaders
article_ideas.based_on: proof indigestion
article_ideas.thesis: Automating generation and verification without automating exposition creates a backlog of valid but unusable proofs; engineering teams should treat human consumption as a first-class pipeline stage with its own metrics and tooling.
article_ideas.title: The Proof Indigestion Problem: Why AI's Verification Success Is Its Exposition Failure
article_ideas.video_title: Terence Tao: SAIR’s Open Math Model Initiative

article_ideas.angle: Architecture decision-making, with evidence from a competition and implications for agent design.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers, ML practitioners, CTOs
article_ideas.based_on: Stage 2 competition winners using open-source LLMs and Python code surprisingly used almost no LLM calls
article_ideas.thesis: In structured problem domains, deterministic solvers and domain encodings should be the default, with LLMs reserved only for ambiguity resolution; defaulting to LLMs is a costly architectural mistake.
article_ideas.title: When Not to Use an LLM: Lessons from a Math Competition Where Winners Called Almost No LLMs
article_ideas.video_title: Terence Tao: SAIR’s Open Math Model Initiative

article_ideas.angle: Data engineering and MLOps, with a call to treat corpus quality as a first-class concern.
article_ideas.audience: Data engineers, ML platform teams, researchers
article_ideas.based_on: Address data pollution caused by uncurated AI-generated mathematical output.
article_ideas.thesis: Uncurated AI-generated output degrades future training and retrieval corpora; provenance tracking and curation gates are reliability infrastructure, not optional features.
article_ideas.title: Data Pollution Is the Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Content: Building Provenance-First Corpora
article_ideas.video_title: Terence Tao: SAIR’s Open Math Model Initiative

article_ideas.angle: Challenge the industry's race toward million-token windows by showing the attention math and practical context engineering alternatives.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers, agent developers, LLM application architects
article_ideas.based_on: A bigger context window is not the fix for context rot.
article_ideas.thesis: Enlarging context windows does not fix context rot because attention quality degrades superlinearly with context size; the correct engineering response is compaction, offloading, and precise retrieval to keep context small and salient.
article_ideas.title: Context Rot Is a Quadratic Attention Problem, Not a Capacity Problem
article_ideas.video_title: Total Recall: Agent Memory and Harness Engineering — Ignacio Martinez, Oracle
